title: Airlines in South America 1920-1942: The German Influence

Airlines in South America 1920-1942: The German Influence

# Airlines in South America 1920-1942: The German Influence

On 25 September 2025, former BEA and British Airways Training Captain, Dacre Watson FRAeS, provided the latest Royal Aeronautical Society (RAeS) Aeronautical Heritage Specialist Group lecture at No.4 Hamilton Place, London.

Titled ‘ Airlines in South America 1920-1942: The German Influence’, his presentation looked at how Germany dominated the region’s airline sector during the interwar years.

Captain Dacre Watson FRAeS addresses the audience at the No.4 Hamilton Place on 25 September. Photography credits: Nigel Dingley MRAeS, Aeronautical Heritage Specialist Group.

Following defeat in WW1, Germany had very onerous restrictions imposed upon it by the Treaty of Versailles – including limitations on aircraft and aero-engine production, as well as the loss of its colonies. Thus, while the victorious European nations developed air routes to their colonies, Germany was forced to look elsewhere to release its aeronautical experience. South America proved attractive, given large ethnic German populations in many of the region’s countries.

Colombia was the first to benefit from the relationship with Germany. Operations by Sociedad Colombo Alemana de Transportes Aéreos (SCADTA) began in 1921, cutting the journey time from the port of Barranquilla to the capital, Bogotá from ten to fourteen days to ten hours.

The founder of SCADTA, Dr Peter Paul von Bauer, worked with German company, Condor Syndicat, a trading firm set up in Berlin in May 1924 for the exclusive purpose of promoting the sale of German commercial aircraft overseas. While von Bauer’s airline was successful, extending to Ecuador by 1928, it caught Juan Trippe’s attention. After the Wall Street crash, Trippe approached von Bauer offering to ‘help’ him by acquiring 50% of SCADTA and taking over the airline’s routes outside of Ecuador. The shareholding was increased to 84% in 1933. The most extraordinary thing about this deal was that it was kept secret by Trippe and von Bauer for many years.

The lecture was lavishly illustrated with period travel posters, maps and images. Image Credits: National Aerospace Library/RAeS.

In Bolivia, Junkers set up Lloyd Aéreo Boliviano (LAB) in 1925, operating Junkers F-13s. Although legally independent of Luft Hansa, it was seen as a subsidiary, operating German aircraft supported by both German personnel and the German-owned Sindicato Condor in Brazil. Luft Hansa expanded into Peru in 1938 operating Junkers Ju 52 aircraft. In Brazil itself, Condor Syndikat (subsidised by Luft Hansa) flew from Buenos Aires to Rio de Janeiro in 1926 and, as a result of this flight, in January 1927, Condor Syndicat was granted a one-year authorisation to operate air services in Brazil. Although Condor Syndicat officially ceased operations in July 1927, Syndicato Condor, the new Brazilian company, simply continued.

Notwithstanding strong German influence within South America, Trippe’s Pan American Airways’ inexorable growth continued. Following his ‘deal’ with SCADTA, and after disposing of Ralf O’Neill’s New York Rio and Buenos Aires Airways (NYBRA) – thus gaining control of the east coast of South America – he formed a joint venture with WR Grace Shipping Line to establish Pan American Grace Airways (PANAGRA) to dominate the west coast.

However, public sentiment and pressures from the US were too great to be ignored. Following the start of WW2 in Europe and subsequent Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor, German influence was finally removed from South American airlines.

Watson’s lecture also addressed transatlantic mail services. This was first conducted by Dornier Wal flying boats to Brazil’s Fernando de Noronha archipelago in the Atlantic, where the mail would be transferred to a fast ship for onward carriage to Las Palmas in Gran Canaria and on to Germany.

In 1934, Wals flew to a ship in mid Atlantic, landing on the ocean before being winched aboard, refuelled and then catapulted off to continue their journey.

Also covered in the lecture were the Zeppelin passenger services from an experimental flight in 1930 to 16 round trips in 1935.

This lecture encompassed a little-known area of aeronautical history in exemplary detail marvellously enlightened by a superb range of photographs, maps and contemporary marketing collateral. Watson will prepare a paper, based upon his lecture, for the Society’s Journal of Aeronautical History.

 Nigel Dingley MRAeS Aeronautical Heritage Specialist Group 17 December 2025
